analysis.one_liner: Bars high earners from adding to retirement accounts above $10 million and speeds up required withdrawals.
analysis.headline: Wyden's bill to limit retirement tax breaks for taxpayers with more than $10 million in retirement savings was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2026 and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop taxpayers earning roughly $400,000 or more from making any new tax-advantaged retirement contributions once their combined retirement balances pass $10 million. It would also force those account holders to withdraw money faster than the usual rules require, so their savings are taxed and spent rather than compounding tax-free indefinitely. It applies to 401(k)s, 403(b)s, government 457 plans, IRAs, and Roth accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers in a general sense: the bill ends an open-ended tax shelter that today can let the wealthiest households pass tens of millions of dollars through tax-advantaged accounts, and it returns some of that deferred tax to the Treasury. It affects a small number of very high earners directly.

how_it_helps.text: Taxpayers with modified adjusted gross income over roughly $400,000-$450,000 (indexed) could make no further contributions to any retirement plan once their aggregate balances exceed $10 million.

Once balances exceed $10 million, required minimum distributions would be increased by 50 percent of the excess over $10 million, forcing faster drawdown and taxation of the savings; once balances exceed $20 million, even Roth money would be included in the required drawdown (though Roth withdrawals would remain tax-free).
The contribution cap takes effect for tax years after 2026, and the accelerated distribution rules take effect for tax years after 2033, giving planners and account holders long notice.
Distributions forced by the new rule would be subject to 37 percent withholding (rather than the usual 10 percent) so the tax is actually collected at the source.

analysis.who_pays: Households with more than $10 million in combined retirement savings and annual income over roughly $400,000. They lose the ability to keep contributing to tax-advantaged accounts and must draw down their balances faster, paying income tax on the withdrawals sooner than they otherwise would.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it touches only taxpayers with very large balances, so it raises relatively little revenue compared with broader retirement or tax reforms, and the bill text itself contains no revenue estimate.

It is technically complex. It layers new definitions, excise taxes, and allocation rules on top of existing law, and it includes a special carve-out for employee stock ownership plans holding untraded employer stock — a sign of the compliance headaches and tailored exceptions that large account holders' advisers would work with.

Forcing drawdowns of Roth money (funded with after-tax dollars) accelerates withdrawals of tax-free savings, which high earners would see as penalizing savings made under rules that previously had no such requirement, since the accelerated distribution rules only start after 2033.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is genuine but modest: it closes a real shelter that lets the wealthiest few compound retirement savings tax-free indefinitely, at little to no cost to anyone earning under roughly $400,000. The cost is added complexity and a late effective date, and it does nothing about the broader gap between households with and without workplace retirement plans. On balance a fair, narrow measure — if it ever moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate on July 21, 2026 and referred to the Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Wyden introduced the bill on July 21, 2026; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, with no cosponsors listed and no further action recorded.
The Finance Committee is chaired by a Republican in this Congress, and no markup or floor action has occurred since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, households with mega retirement accounts — the bill sits untouched in committee with no cosponsors.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it referred to the Finance Committee, where he has served as a senior member and former chair.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after it was referred to the committee; no markup was scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or committee action exist to show a split; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: They would lose unlimited tax-advantaged compounding and be forced to draw down and pay tax on balances sooner. The cost falls on a small group with the largest concentrated tax benefit.

industries.industry: Wealth management and retirement plan administration
industries.note: The rules would create new compliance and allocation work for plans and advisers, while forced withdrawals would move some assets from tax-advantaged accounts to taxable ones, changing — not necessarily shrinking — managed assets.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is in the Senate Finance Committee with no cosponsors and no scheduled action, with the Congress ending in January 2027. Bills at this stage — a lone sponsor, no committee markup — almost never become law, and the odds here are effectively nil in the remaining weeks of the session.
